'''Anthony James Pawson''' (18 October 1952 – 7 August 2013<ref name="natureobit">{{Cite journal | last1 = Bernstein | first1 = Alan| author-link1 = Alan Bernstein| last2 = Rossant | first2 = Janet| author-link2 = Janet Rossant| doi = 10.1038/501168a | title = Anthony James Pawson (1952–2013) Biochemist whose vision of cell signalling transformed cancer research| journal = Nature | volume = 501 | issue = 7466 | page = 168 | year = 2013 | pmid =  24025833| doi-access = free | bibcode = 2013Natur.501..168B }}</ref>) was a British-born Canadian genetic scientist. He was known and recognized for his work on cellular organization, including how cells respond to growth signals, and how they communicate with each other.<ref name="NYTPawson"/>

Pawson is the recipient of several notable awards such as [[Gairdner Foundation International Award]], [[Wolf Prize in Medicine]], [[Thomson Reuters Citation Laureates]] and [[Kyoto Prize]].

==Biography==
Pawson was born in [[Maidstone]], England.<ref name="natureobit"/> He was the son of the sportsman and writer [[Tony Pawson (cricketer)|Tony Pawson]], and botanist and high-school teacher Hilarie. He was the eldest of three children.<ref>{{cite news|author=Buck, Genna |date=14 August 2013 |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/life/health-and-fitness/health/anthony-pawson-helped-discover-how-cells-communicate-with-each-other/article13778193/ |title=Anthony Pawson helped discover how cells communicate with each other |newspaper=[[The Globe and Mail]] |access-date=5 May 2014}}</ref>

He studied at the [[Winchester College]]<ref>{{cite web|last1=Kyriakis|first1=John M.|title=Retrospective Tony Pawson (1952–2013)|url=http://www.asbmb.org/asbmbtoday/asbmbtoday_article.aspx?id=48920|publisher=ASBMB Today|access-date=16 January 2015}}</ref> and [[Clare College, Cambridge]], where he received an [[Master of Arts (Oxbridge)|MA]] in biochemistry followed by a PhD from [[King's College London]] in 1976. From 1976 to 1980 he pursued postdoctoral work at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. From 1981 to 1985, he was assistant professor in microbiology at the [[University of British Columbia]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Tony Pawson, renowned Canadian scientist, dies at 60 |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/tony-pawson-renowned-canadian-scientist-dies-at-60-1.1301463 |work=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation|CBC]] |date=9 August 2013}}</ref><ref name="Nature">{{cite journal |last1=Heldin |first1=Carl-Henrik |last2=Scott |first2=John |title=Tony Pawson 1952–2013 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/ncb2854 |journal=Nature Cell Biology |date=October 2013 |volume=15 |issue=10 |page=1134 |language=en |doi=10.1038/ncb2854|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Pawson was a Distinguished Investigator and former Director of Research at the [[Samuel Lunenfeld Research Institute]] of [[Mount Sinai Hospital (Toronto)|Mount Sinai Hospital]] and Professor in the Department of Molecular Genetics at the [[University of Toronto]] both of which he joined in 1985.<ref>{{cite news |title=In Memoriam: Anthony Pawson |url=https://magazine.utoronto.ca/people/faculty-staff/in-memoriam-anthony-pawson-jim-woodgett-lunenfeld-tanenbaum-research-institute-mount-sinai-hospital/ |work=University of Toronto Magazine |date=1 December 2013 |language=en-CA}}</ref>

Pawson died on 7 August 2013 of unspecified causes at the age of 60.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.thestar.com/life/health_wellness/2013/08/08/renowned_toronto_genetic_researcher_dr_tony_pawson_dies.html |title=Renowned Toronto genetic researcher Dr. Tony Pawson dies &#124; Toronto Star |work=Thestar.com |date= 8 August 2013|access-date=9 August 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | title=Scientific community reels at the loss of the world-renowned Tony Pawson | url=http://www.macleans.ca/2013/08/09/scientific-community-reels-at-the-loss-of-the-world-renowned-tony-pawson/ | work=Maclean's | date=9 August 2013 | access-date=10 August 2013}}
</ref><ref>{{cite news | author=Paul Wells| title=RIP Tony Pawson | url=http://www.macleans.ca/2013/08/09/rip-tony-pawson/ | work=Maclean's | date=9 August 2013 | access-date=10 August 2013}}</ref><ref name="NYTPawson">{{cite news |last1=Vitello |first1=Paul |title=Anthony Pawson, Biologist in Cell-Protein Breakthrough, Dies at 60 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/08/30/world/americas/anthony-pawson-biologist-in-cell-protein-breakthrough-dies-at-60.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=29 August 2013}}</ref>

==Research==

Pawson's research changed the understanding of [[signal transduction]], the molecular mechanisms by which cells respond to external cues, and how they communicate with each other. He identified the phosphotyrosine-binding Src homology 2 ([[SH2 domain]]) as the prototypic non-catalytic interaction module. SH2 domains serve as a model for a large family of protein modules that act together to control many aspects of cellular signalling. Since the discovery of SH2 domains, hundreds of different modules have been identified in many proteins.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Pawson | first1 = T. | last2 = Nash | first2 = P. | title = Assembly of Cell Regulatory Systems Through Protein Interaction Domains | doi = 10.1126/science.1083653 | journal = Science | volume = 300 | issue = 5618 | pages = 445–452 | year = 2003 | pmid =  12702867| s2cid = 14634947 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Nash | first1 = P. | last2 = Tang | first2 = X. | last3 = Orlicky | first3 = S. | last4 = Chen | first4 = Q. | last5 = Gertler | first5 = F. ==Honours and awards==
* 1994 - [[Gairdner Foundation International Award]]
* 1994 - Fellow of the [[Royal Society of London]] and the [[Royal Society of Canada]]
* 1995 – [[Robert L. Noble Prize]] from the National Cancer Institute of Canada
* 1998 – Pezcoller-AACR International Award for Cancer Research
* 1998 – [[Heineken Prize]] for Biochemistry and Biophysics, [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]]
* 1998 – The Royal Society of Canada Flavelle Medal for meritorious achievement in biological science
* 2000 – J. Allyn Taylor International Prize in Medicine<ref>{{cite news |title=Exceptional contributions to cancer research recognized |url=https://healthenews.mcgill.ca/exceptional-contributions-to-cancer-research-recognized/ |work=Health e-News |date=25 November 2011 |language=en-CA}}</ref>
* 2004 – [[Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize]] from [[Columbia University]]
* 2004 – Poulsson Medal, the Norwegian Society of Pharmacology and Toxicology
* 2004 – Associate of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (US)
* 2004 – Member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]
* 2005 – [[Wolf Prize in Medicine]] "for his discovery of protein domains essential for mediating protein-protein interactions in cellular signaling pathways, and the insights this research has provided into cancer"
* 2005 – The [[Royal Medal]] (The Queen's Medal) from The [[Royal Society of London]]
* 2006 – [[Member of the Order of the Companions of Honour]]
* 2007 – Premiers Summit Award
* 2007 – [[Howard Taylor Ricketts|Howard Taylor Ricketts Award]] from [[University of Chicago]]
* 2008 [[Kyoto Prize]]  – "Japan's Nobel" for "Proposing and Proving the Concept of Adapter Molecules in the Signal Transduction"
* 2012 – Clarivate Citation Laureate<ref name="Hall of Fame">{{cite news |title=Anthony Pawson – Canadian Medical Hall of Fame |url=https://www.cdnmedhall.ca/laureates/anthonypawson# |work=www.cdnmedhall.ca |language=en}}</ref>
* 2012 – [[Thomson Reuters Citation Laureates]], candidate for Nobel Prize in Medicine "for identification of the phosphotyrosine binding SH2 domain and demonstrating its function in protein-protein interactions"
* 2013 – Annual award of the Canadian National Proteomics Network, thereafter named the ''CNPN-Tony Pawson Proteomics Award''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnpn.ca/about/past_award_winners.html|title=Past award winners|website=Canadian National Proteomics Network|access-date=16 July 2019}}</ref><ref name="Hall of Fame" />
